new_projects.title: Glycopeptide analysis of A549 cells after influenza A infection
new_projects.description: Influenza A virus (IAV) hijacks host cellular machinery, but many virus–IAV interactions and contacting protein sites remain uncharacterised, particularly those dependent on intact cellular architecture, such as membrane-associated or phase-separated compartments. Here, we applied in-cell cross-linking mass spectrometry (XL-MS), integrated with AlphaFold-based structural modelling and functional assays, to map protein-protein contact sites in IAV-infected human cells.
new_projects.sample_processing_protocol: Lysis of cells with a strong lysis buffer, then digestion with trypsin. Glyco peptides were enriched using PBA beads. Both full proteome and glyco proteome were pre-fractionated after TMT labeling and analysed with LC-MSMS.
new_projects.data_processing_protocol: Generated raw files were searched using MSFragger v4.0 in Fragpipe v20.0 against the Swissprot Homo sapiens database (UP000005640, 20,443 entries) combined with the influenza A database (UP000009255, 13 entries).  For the quantitative analysis of proteomics and glycoproteomics data, we first normalized the TMT reporter intensities for glycopeptides and proteins with complete quantification across all conditions (i.e. TMT reporter ion intensity different from 0 for all channels) using the normalizeVSN function of the limma R package. We corrected glycopeptide intensities per protein by removing abundance-derived intensity using a linear regression for all glycopeptides with a matched total protein intensity. The corrected and normalized glycopeptide intensities as well as the normalized protein intensities were used for the differential analysis using the limma R package. For the design of the DE analysis, we considered the knockdown condition as well as the sample replicate. Contrasts were set for the comparison of the non-targeting control against respective knockdown conditions.

new_projects.title: BioID2 interactome of wild-type SYCP1 versus the D918–942 mutant
new_projects.description: This dataset comprises a tandem mass tag (TMT)–based quantitative proteomic analysis of proteins proximal to SYCP1 identified using BioID proximity labelling. Two independent BioID experiments were performed using distinct SYCP1 constructs: an N-terminal Myc-tagged SYCP1 and a C-terminal HA-tagged SYCP1. For each construct, full-length wild-type SYCP1, a SYCP1 deletion mutant lacking amino acids 918–942, and a SYCP1 knockout negative control were analysed in MCF7 cells. Biotinylated proteins were enriched by streptavidin-based affinity purification, and the resulting protein lysates were submitted to the EMBL Proteomics Core Facility for downstream processing and LC–MS/MS analysis, enabling quantitative comparison of SYCP1-associated proteins across constructs and conditions.
new_projects.sample_processing_protocol: Cells expressing either N-terminal Myc-tagged or C-terminal HA-tagged SYCP1 constructs were cultured under standard conditions and subjected to BioID proximity labelling. Biotinylated proteins were enriched using streptavidin-based affinity purification, and enriched protein lysates were collected for mass spectrometry analysis. Protein samples were subjected to the SP3 protocol (PMID 25358341) conducted on the KingFisher Apex™ platform (Thermo Fisher). For digestion, trypsin was used in a 1:20 ratio (protease:protein) in 50 mM N-2-hydroxyethylpiperazine-N-2-ethanesulfonic acid (HEPES) supplemented with 5 mM Tris(2-carboxyethyl)phosphine hydrochloride (TCEP) and 20 mM 2-chloroacetamide (CAA). Digestion was carried out for 5 hours at 37°C.  Peptides were labeled using TMTpro™ 16plex reagent as previously described (PMID: 31738517). Briefly, 0.5 mg of TMT reagent was dissolved in 45 µL of 100% acetonitrile. Subsequently, 4 µL of this solution was added to each peptide sample, followed by incubation at room temperature for 1 hour. The labeling reaction was quenched by adding 4 µL of a 5% aqueous hydroxylamine solution and incubating for an additional 15 minutes at room temperature. La
new_projects.data_processing_protocol: Raw files were converted to mzML format using MSConvert from ProteoWizard, using peak picking, 64-bit encoding and zlib compression, and filtering for the 1000 most intense peaks. Files were then searched using MSFragger (v4.0) in FragPipe (21.1) against the FASTA database of homo sapiens (UP000005640; ID9606; 20594 entries; October 2022) containing common contaminants and reversed sequences. The following modifications were included into the search parameters: Carbamidomethylation (C, 57.0215), TMTpro (K, 304.2072) as fixed modifications; Oxidation (M, 15.9949), Acetylation (protein N-terminus, 42.0106), TMTpro (peptide N-terminus, 304.2072) as variable modifications. For the full scan (MS1) a mass error tolerance of 20 PPM and for MS/MS (MS2) spectra of 20 PPM was set. For protein digestion, 'stricttrypsin' was used as protease with an allowance of maximum 2 missed cleavages requiring a minimum peptide length of 7 amino acids. The false discovery rate on peptide and protein level was set to 0.01.

new_projects.description: This project investigates the impact of N-myristoyltransferase (NMT) inhibition on the myristoylated proteome of Trypanosoma cruzi and human cardiomyocytes in the context of Chagas disease. Human AC16 cardiomyocytes were infected with T. cruzi (CL Brener strain) and treated with the reference NMT inhibitor DDD85646 or vehicle control. Myristoylated proteins from intracellular amastigotes, extracellular trypomastigotes, and host cells were metabolically labeled with an azide-functionalized myristic acid analogue, enriched by click-chemistry, digested, and labeled with TMTsixplex reagents for multiplexed quantification. Labeled peptide fractions were analyzed by nanoLC–MS/MS on a Vanquish Neo UHPLC coupled to an Orbitrap Exploris 240 operated in data-dependent acquisition mode. The resulting
new_projects.sample_processing_protocol: AC16 human cardiomyocytes (Thermo Fisher Scientific, AC16 cell line) were cultured under standard conditions and infected with T. cruzi CL Brener trypomastigotes at an MOI of 10:1. After invasion and washing, infected cultures were incubated ± DDD85646 for 72 h. Intracellular amastigotes and released trypomastigotes were isolated by differential centrifugation and DEAE-cellulose chromatography, and parasite numbers and purity were verified microscopically. For metabolic labeling, cultures were supplemented for the final 16 h with 50 µM Click-iT myristic acid, azide (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Cells and parasites were lysed in Click-iT lysis buffer with protease inhibitors, clarified by centrifugation, and azide-labeled proteins were captured on alkyne-agarose resin using the Click-iT Protein Enrichment Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Resin-bound proteins were reduced with DTT, alkylated with iodoacetamide, and digested on-resin with sequencing-grade trypsin at 37 °C. Peptides from each condition were labeled with TMTsixplex™ reagents (Thermo Fisher Scientific), combined, and fractionated using the Pierce™ High-pH Reversed-Phase Peptide F
new_projects.data_processing_protocol: Raw files were processed in Proteome Discoverer v2.5 (Thermo Fisher Scientific) using the Sequest HT search engine. Spectra were searched against a combined Homo sapiens (UniProt UP000005640) and Trypanosoma cruzi (taxon 5693) database supplemented with common contaminants. Carbamidomethylation of cysteine and TMTsixplex modifications on peptide N-termini and lysine residues were set as fixed modifications; oxidation of methionine and N-terminal acetylation were set as variable. Peptide-spectrum matches and protein identifications were filtered to 1% FDR using a target–decoy strategy and Percolator. TMT reporter-ion intensities (m/z 126–131) were extracted, corrected for isotopic impurities, and normalized across channels for relative quantification. Differential protein abundance was assessed using non-parametric statistical tests with Benjamini–Hochberg correction (q < 0.05). Processed datasets were imported into Scaffold DDA v6.5 (Proteome Software) for additional validation and visualization. Proteins were screened for N-terminal glycine motifs, and candidate N-myristoylated proteins were further evaluated using the ExPASy Myristoylator prediction tool.

new_projects.title: Proteomic Profiling of Human Epileptic Tissue
new_projects.description: This project describes the proteomic profiling of human epilepic brain tissue, alongside control samples. Microdissected hippocampal, neocortical, and white matter tissue was analyzed. The aim was to identify protein alterations associated for different epileptic conditions. Raw mass spectrometry data, along with search engine output, are included in this partial submission.
new_projects.sample_processing_protocol: Fresh-frozen brain tissue was homogenized in lysis buffer and beads. Protein extraction was done by adding lysis and digestion buffer with trypsin. Peptides were labeled with TMT-16-plex reagents for quantification. LC-MS/MS analysis was done by injecting peptides into Orbitrap Eclipse mass spectrometer and full-MS spectra were collected.
new_projects.data_processing_protocol: Raw MS files were processed with Proteome Discoverer 2.4 (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Spectra were matched against Homo Sapiens database obtained from UniProt. All results were filtered to a 1% FDR. Search engine output files and raw mass spectrometry files included.

new_projects.sample_processing_protocol: Tissue samples were sectioned using a microtome (7 μm thick), transferred into 1.5 mL tubes and deparaffinized by incubation with xylol for 30 min. After the addition of methanol, samples were vortexed thoroughly and centrifuged for 2 min (15,000 rpm). The supernatant was removed, and tissue samples were air-dried followed by resuspension in RIPA buffer with protease/phosphatase inhibitors. Samples were boiled and sonicated, followed by heating for 2 h at 80 °C (500 rpm). Protein digestion was performed using the Thermo Scientific™ EasyPep™ Mini MS Sample Preparation Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific, A40006) following the manufacturer's protocol. The resulting protein extracts were then subjected to reduction and alkylation steps. Subsequently, proteins were digested into peptides using the reconstituted Trypsin/Lys-C Protease Mix with an incubation at 37°C overnight. The digestion was terminated by the addition of the Digestion Stop Solution. Finally, the resulting peptides were purified and concentrated using the provided peptide clean-up columns. TMT reagents (0.8 mg) were dissolved in acetonitrile (40 μL), of which 20 μL was added to the peptides (50 μg). Peptide quantification wa
new_projects.data_processing_protocol: Mass spectra were searched against all entries from the human UniProt Database (downloaded: August 2021) using MaxQuant (version 1.7.1.0). Trypsin/P was specified as a cleavage enzyme, allowing up to two missed cleavages and a mass tolerance of 20 ppm Orbitrap for precur sor ions and MS2 fragment ions. The product mass tolerance was set to 0.5 Da, and a maximum of two missed tryptic cleavages were allowed. Carbamidomethylation of cysteine was used as a fixed modification, with the oxidation of methionine and acetylation of lysine residue used as variable modifications. A reverse nonsense version of the original  database was generated and used to determine the FDR, which was set to 1% for peptide identifications. Reporter ion intensities were adjusted to correct for the isotopic impurities of the different TMT reagents according to manufacturer specifications. Missing value imputations were carried out from a normal distribution (width: 0.3, downshift: 1.8) using Perseus software. The normalization of reporter ion intensities was carried with an internal reference scaling (IRS) method.

Cells were maintained in a humidified incubator at 37 °C and 5% CO2. Next, ten million of KM12L4a cells were seeded on a 75 mm equilibrated PAAm gel at approximately 1.5x106 cells/cm² and cultured for 24 h in a humidified incubator at 37 °C and 5% CO2. For starvation, cells were washed twice with 10 mL prewarmed DPBS (1x Thermo Fisher, 14190144) and transferred to a new Petri dish to remove runoff cells. The gel was washed again and incubated in 13 mL prewarmed serum-free medium for 48 h to eliminate serum interference.  Starved cell medium was collected, centrifuged (5 min, 140 g) to remove dead cells, and frozen at -80 °C. A 10 mL portion was concentrated 10x via freeze-drying and resuspended in 1 mL sterile MilliQ water for analysis. new_projects.data_processing_protocol: LC-MS/MS analysis was performed using an Orbitrap Exploris 480 mass spectrometer coupled with a Vanquish Neo UHPLC System for peptide separation (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Peptides were analyzed with a 2-hour gradient using 0.1% FA in MQ and 0.1% FA in 80% ACN as buffers.  Mass spectra were searched against the Uniprot Homo sapiens database using MaxQuant (v2.4.2), with trypsin as the digestion enzyme and stringent FDR thresholds of 0.01 for peptide identification. Protein quantification was performed with reporter ion intensities bias-corrected for TMT reagents. Statistical analysis included Bayes-moderated t-tests and filtering for proteins identified in ≥60% of samples, with significant dysregulated proteins defined by expression ratio cutoffs of ≥1.5 or ≤0.67 and FDR ≤0.05. Dysregulated proteins were further analyzed for secretion pathways using SecretomeP 2.0, SignalP 6.0, and the ExoCarta database.

new_projects.title: Proteomic analysis of Prote-a-Tac
new_projects.description: The 26S proteasome recognizes substrates via ubiquitin receptors, a mechanism we leveraged to develop a small molecule ligand- and ubiquitination-independent targeted protein degradation strategy. Our proteasome-targeting chimera, Prote-a-Tac, links a proteasomal Ub receptor (PSMD4 or ADRM1) with a target-specific antibody fragment (such as a scFv or nanobody), allowing it to integrate into the proteasome and promote ubiquitin-independent   degradation.   The   Prote-a-Tac   platform   demonstrated   high specificity and minimal off-target effects, as confirmed by quantitative mass spectrometry.
new_projects.sample_processing_protocol: A549 cells were transfected with scFv(HA)–ADRM1 (negative control 1), ADRM1–HTB & scFv(c-Fos)–HTB (negative control 2), or scFv(c-Fos)–ADRM1 (experimental group)(n = 5), cultured, harvested, washed with PBS, and snap-frozen. Cell pellets were lysed in 4 % SDS and 0.1 M Tris-HCl (pH 8.0), boiled, sonicated, centrifuged, and quantified by BCA. 40 µg of protein were acetone-precipitated, then resuspended in buffer with 5 % SDS, reduced (TCEP), and alkylated (CAA). After acidification, samples were loaded onto S-Trap columns, washed, and digested on-column with trypsin. Peptides were eluted, TMTpro-labeled, pooled, C18-cleaned, fractionated into 24 fractions, and stored at −80 °C.
new_projects.data_processing_protocol: Raw files were analyzed in Proteome Discoverer 3.1 using Sequest HT with a 1 % FDR cutoff and standard TMT settings. Spectra with high interference or low S/N were removed; proteins with ≥3 unique peptides were quantified. In Perseus, log₂-transformed intensities were normalized, and t-tests (FDR < 0.05, fold-change ≥ 1.2) identified differentially expressed proteins.

Approximately 1µg of peptide was separated at a flow rate of 450 nL/min across 90 minutes on a 100 µm capillary column that was packed with 35 cm of Accucore 150 resin (2.6 μm, 150Å; ThermoFisher Scientific). The gradient was 7-25% Buffer B (95% acetonitrile, 0.125% formic acid) which was mixed into buffer A (5% acetonitrile, 0.125% formic acid). The scan sequence began with an MS1 spectrum (Orbitrap analysis, resolution 60,000, 350-1350 Th, automatic gain control (AGC) target is set to 100%, maximum injection time set to 50ms). new_projects.data_processing_protocol: Spectra were converted to mzXML via MSconvert and searched using Comet against the human canonical proteome (Uniprot 2020-02). Searches were performed using a 50-ppm precursor ion tolerance for total protein level profiling. The product ion tolerance was set to 0.03 Da. These wide mass tolerance windows were chosen to maximize sensitivity in conjunction with Comet searches and linear discriminant analysis. TMTpro labels on lysine residues and peptide N-termini +304.207 Da), as well as carbamidomethylation of cysteine residues (+57.021 Da) were set as static modifications, while oxidation of methionine residues (+15.995 Da) was set as a variable modification. Linear discriminant analysis was performed and peptide-spectrum matches (PSMs) were filtered to 2% false discovery rate (FDR). TMT-reporter ions were quantified by picking the most intense peaks within 0.003 Da around the theoretical m/z and corrected for isotopic impurity. The remaining homogenate underwent a low-speed centrifugation (700× g) (5415D centrifuge, Eppendorf North America, Hauppauge, NY, USA) for 10 min at 4 °C to separate the intact nuclei and heavy membranes (pellet 1) from the supernatant (supernatant 1). new_projects.data_processing_protocol: Database Search Peptide tandem MS data were processed using Sequest [Thermo Fisher Scientific, San Jose, CA, in Proteome Discoverer (PD) 2.5]. new_projects.description: Tissues were collected during the Amsterdam (Netherlands) study of Carbohydrate Regulation of Lipid Metabolism ("SODA").  Subjects were divided between those with and without Metabolic Dysfunction Associated Steatotic Liver Disease (MASLD); subjects were further divided by insulin resistance as assessed by hyperinsulinemic-euglycemic clamp.  Prior to bariatric surgery, subjects were given a glucose or fructose drink.  Subcutaneous and omental adipose tissues were collected during bariatric surgery.  Proteomic data was collected from both subcutaneous and omental adipose tissue; and from subjects given either carbohydrate drink (fructose or glucose).
new_projects.sample_processing_protocol: Frozen tissue biopsies were processed using the streamlined TMT labelling protocol (Navarrete-Perea et al., 2018). Processing included lysis with 8M urea in 200mM EPPS pH 8.5 with protease (Pierce A32953) and phosphatase (Pierce A32957) inhibitors, reduction with 5mM TCEP, alkylation with 10mM iodoacetamide, and quenching with 5mM DTT. This was followed by methanol/chloroform precipitation of 100μg of protein, reconstitution in 200mM EPPS pH 8.5, digestion overnight at room temperature with 1:100 LysC (Wako 129-02541), and digestion with 1:100 trypsin (Pierce 90305) at 37°C. Peptides were labelled by adding anhydrous acetonitrile (Honeywell AS017-0100) to ~30%, followed by labelling with TMTpro (Thermo A44520) reagent. A small amount of each sample (20ug) was combined to make a bridge channel. 1% of each labeled sample was combined and analyzed unfractionated to ensure labeling efficiency was >97% and that the samples are mixed at a 1:1 (total amount) ratio across all conditions. After mixing, labelled peptide samples were de-salted using a 200mg Sep-Pak cartridge (Waters WAT054925), followed by drying in a rotary evaporator. Peptides were reconstituted in 5% ACN 10mM ammonium bica
new_projects.data_processing_protocol: Mass spectra were processed using a COMET-based software pipeline. Data were searched against the UniProt Human database (June 2021), using a 20-ppm precursor ion tolerance for total protein-level analysis and 0.9 Da product ion tolerance. TMTpro and carbamidomethylation of cysteine were set as static modifications, while methionine oxidation and asparagine/glutamine deamidaion as variable modifications. Peptide-spectrum matches (PSMs) were identified, quantified, and filtered to a 1% peptide false discovery rate (FDR) and then collapsed further to a final protein-level FDR of 1%. Proteins were quantified by summing reporter ion counts across all matching PSMs. Briefly, a 0.003 Da (3 millidalton) window around the theoretical m/z of each reporter ion was scanned and the maximum intensity nearest the theoretical m/z was used. Reporter ion intensities were adjusted to correct for the isotopic impurities of the different TMT reagents according to manufacturer specifications and adjusted to normalize ratios across labelling channels. Lastly, for each protein, signal-to-noise (S:N) measurements of the peptides were summed and then normalized to 100.

new_projects.sample_processing_protocol: MCF-7 (ER+) and MDA-MB-231 (ER-) cells were cultured in standard growth media and treated with Licochalcone A (LicA) (10 µM) for 24 hours or DMSO as a control. new_projects.data_processing_protocol: Raw LC-MS/MS data were processed using Proteome Discoverer, and protein abundances were normalized based on TMT reporter ion intensities. new_projects.title: DMXL1 interaction proteomics from U2OS cells
new_projects.description: To identify protein interactions with DMXL1, U2OS cells were engineered to either stably over-express DMXL1 tagged with mNeonGreen (mNG) or express HA-dTAG-tagged DMXL1 from the endogenous locus. Tagged DMXL1 was pulled-down by immunoprecipitation (IP) and IP samples were processed for TMT-MS analysis. As negative control, pull-down was also performed from parental U2OS cells. Each condition was performed in triplicate.
new_projects.sample_processing_protocol: DMXL1-IP samples were reduced with 5mM TCEP, alkylated with 15mM iodoacetamide, and quenched with 10mM DTT. Proteins were digested with Lys-C/Trypsin and digested peptides were labelled with TMTpro reagent for 1h at room temperature and reaction was quenched with hydroxylamine for 15min. Equal amounts of peptide were combined and desalted using C18 StageTip. Samples were analyzed by LC-MS/MS on an Orbitrap Eclipse or Fusion Lumos Tribrid mass spectrometer coupled with an nLC-1200 or Vanquish Neo liquid chromatograph. Peptides were separated on a 100µm inner diameter microcapillary column packed with approximately 35cm of Accucore C18 resin (2.6µm, 150Å, Thermo), over a 90-min linear gradient of acetonitrile. MS1 spectrum was acquired on the Orbitrap (resolution 60,000, scan range 350-1,350 m/z, 100% AGC target, 118ms maximum injection time). MS2 was acquired on the Orbitrap (resolution 50,000, isolation window 0.6 m/z, 36% normalized HCD collision energy, 200% normalized AGC, 120ms maximum injection time). FAIMS Pro was set to -30, -50 and -70 compensation voltage (CV). FAIMS was set to -40, -60 and-80 CV for the second run.
new_projects.data_processing_protocol: Spectra were converted to mzXML via MSconvert and searched using Comet against the human canonical proteome (Uniprot 2020-02). Searches were performed using a 50-ppm precursor ion tolerance for total protein level profiling. The product ion tolerance was set to 0.03 Da. These wide mass tolerance windows were chosen to maximize sensitivity in conjunction with Comet searches and linear discriminant analysis. TMTpro labels on lysine residues and peptide N-termini +304.207 Da), as well as carbamidomethylation of cysteine residues (+57.021 Da) were set as static modifications, while oxidation of methionine residues (+15.995 Da) was set as a variable modification. Linear discriminant analysis was performed and peptide-spectrum matches (PSMs) were filtered to 2% false discovery rate (FDR). TMT-reporter ions were quantified by picking the most intense peaks within 0.003 Da around the theoretical m/z and corrected for isotopic impurity. Data summarization, normalization and statistics were performed using MSstats.

new_projects.data_processing_protocol: Proteome Discoverer 3.0 (Thermo Scientific) was used with SequestHT and Comet search engines for protein identification and quantification. Spectra were searched against Homo sapiens protein entries in UniProt, with a precursor mass tolerance of 20 ppm and a fragment mass tolerance of 0.02 Da. Fully tryptic peptides were considered, allowing up to 2 missed cleavages. Static modifications were TMT at N-termini/K and carbamidomethylation at C residues. Dynamic modifications included oxidation of methionine, and deamidation of N/Q.  Peptide confidence was estimated using Percolator, maintaining a false discovery rate (FDR) of 1% with target-decoy database validation. new_projects.title: The temporal dynamics of proteins in aged skin wound healing and comparison to gene expression
new_projects.description: Wound healing, a multifaceted process, often leads to chronic wounds when disrupted. Predominantly, research in this area has relied on in vitro or animal models, which potentially oversimplify the intricacies of human wound healing. This simplification could contribute to the current gap in effective clinical therapies and prognostic tools. Our study aims to deepen the understanding of human skin wound healing mechanisms at the temporal protein level. Utilizing labeled mass spectrometry, we quantified the proteome of full-thickness skin samples at both acute and late healing stages from legs of 14 healthy individuals.   Our results revealed distinct proteomic profiles corresponding to different wound healing days, indicating a unique protein signature for each stage. Functional enrichment
new_projects.sample_processing_protocol: Proteins were extracted from biopsy samples using the ProteaseMAX/urea protocol™ (Promega) to ensure high yield. Samples were prepared by using an in-solution tryptic digestion protocol, including reduction and alkylation of S-S bonds. Later, they were subjected to a TMT labeling strategy, allowing for multiplexing of biological samples (up to 16 using TMTpro).
new_projects.data_processing_protocol: TMT-labeled samples were analyzed in a data-dependent manner, using MS2 (tandem mass spectrometry) sequence-specific fragments of peptides simultaneously with TMT reporter ions used for relative quantification. For deep proteome profiling, high pH reversed-phase fractionation was performed on TMT-labeled samples, and 12 concatenated fractions were analyzed to reach 6-7000 protein proteome depth in a combined analysis of the fractions. Protein identification was performed using H. sapiens database. The detected proteins were filtered by applying a 1% False Discovery Rate (FDR) cut-off. Proteome Discoverer™ (ThermoFisher Scientific) was used to determine relative protein abundances in the sample groups, by setting up a TMTpro quantification method (MS2-based). The protein abundance ratios were calculated as fold changes using median values for each group. The p-values were determined using Student’s t-test adjusted for multiple hypotheses.

new_projects.title: Quantitative proteomics analysis of UBR4 knockout A549 cell line
new_projects.description: UBR4 was identified as a potential oncogene in lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD). In this study, we performed a quantitative proteomics analysis using tandem mass tag (TMT) 6-plex technology in UBR4 knockout A549 cell lines to discover an essential role of UBR4 in tumor growth and metastasis.
new_projects.sample_processing_protocol: A549 cell pellets were lysed in lysis buffer (4% SDS, 2 mM TCEP, and 0.1 M tris-HCl, pH 7.5) by direct sonication (10%, 3 cycles, 5 s, 2 s). Lysates were heated for 30 min at 95 °C. To minimize interference from the reducing reagent, the concentration of proteins was measured using a reducing agent-compatible BCA assay (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA). Then, each sample containing 300 μg of total protein was precipitated with cold acetone. Samples were re-suspended in denaturation buffer (2% sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS), 10 mM tris(2-carboxyethyl)phosphine (TCEP), 50 mM chloroacetamide (CAA), and 0.1 M tris-HCl, pH 8.5) and heated for 15 min at 95 °C. The proteins were digested via multidigestion filter-aided sample preparation according to our previously described process.
new_projects.data_processing_protocol: Raw MS/MS files were processed with Proteome Discoverer ver 2.5 (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA), using the SEQUEST HT algorithms against the Human Uniprot protein sequence database (December_2019). The database search parameters were as follows: full enzyme digest using trypsin (after KR/-) with up to two missed cleavages allowed; a precursor ion mass tolerance of 20 ppm; a fragment ion mass tolerance of 0.02 Da; dynamic modifications of 15.995 Da for methionine oxidation and 42.011 Da for protein N-term acetylation; and static modifications of 57.021 Da for carbamidomethylation on cysteine residues and 229.153 Da for TMT 6plex on any N-terminus. The co-isolation threshold was set to 50%. Six reporter ion intensities for TMT were corrected for isotopic impurities as provided by the manufacturer. Peptide spectral matches and peptides were confirmed by a Percolator based on a 1% false discovery rate (FDR). Confidence criteria were set to a 1% FDR at the protein level.

MSGF+ settings included precursor mass tolerance of 10 ppm, fully-tryptic peptides, maximum peptide length of 50 amino acids and a maximum charge of 6. Fixed modifications were TMT-10plex on lysines and peptide N-termini, and carbamidomethylation on cysteine residues, a variable modification was used for oxidation on methionine residues. Protein quantification by TMT10plex reporter ions was calculated using TMT PSM ratios to the entire sample set (all 10 TMT-channels) and normalized to the sample median.

new_projects.sample_processing_protocol: Thirty-nine patients from the discovery cohort were randomly distributed into three batches (Table S2). Proteins were extracted from FFPE tissue specimens of these patients and digested by Pressure Cycling Technology (PCT) assisted proteomic sample preparation as described previously (PMID: 35931778, 33503446). Peptides from each of the 39 specimens, six randomly selected technical replicates (including three intra-batch and three inter-batch replicates), and three common pooled samples samples were labeled with TMTpro 16plex reagent (Thermo Fisher Scientific, San Jose, USA) (Table S2). The combined sample of each batch was fractionated as described previously (PMID: 33503446). A total of 60 fractions were collected by high-pH reversed-phase fractionation and concatenated into 30 fractions. After dried under vacuum, peptides were separated in a 60-min gradient by Thermo ScientificTM UltiMateTM 3000 RSLCnano System and analyzed using an Orbitrap Exploris 480 mass spectrometry with FAIMS Pro interface in data-dependent acquisition (DDA) mode. The detailed settings of MS have been described previously (PMID: 35110523).
new_projects.data_processing_protocol: The raw data were analyzed by Proteome Discoverer software (Version 2.4.0.305, Thermo Fisher Scientific) against a FASTA file containing 20,368 reviewed Homo sapiens proteins downloaded from UniProt website on 15 July 2020 as described previously (PMID: 33503446). Briefly, trypsin was chosen as the enzyme for peptide generation, allowing a maximum of 2 missed cleavages. The mass tolerance for precursor ions was set at 10 ppm, while the tolerance for fragment ions was set at 0.02 Da. Variable modifications included oxidation (M) and acetyl (protein N-terminus), while carbamidomethyl (C) was set as a static modification. Further analysis was conducted on proteins and peptides with false discovery rates below 1% that were quantified.

Tumour regions across the length of each core were circled on the H&E slide, matched to the block of cores, and cored a second time with a 1.0 mm punch or 0.5 mm punch. The ‘cored cores’ with enriched tumour were placed in their respective microcentrifuge tubes for each sample.

new_projects.title: Discovery and Development of CD70 As a Cellular Therapy Target in High Risk Multiple Myeloma
new_projects.description: Even in the BCMA CAR-T era, multiple myeloma (MM) patients with high-risk genotypes have the poorest outcomes. We thus leveraged MMRF CoMMpass data to identify potential novel surface immunotherapeutic targets in high-risk MM. As described below, we focused on CD70, an immunotherapeutic target known to be upregulated on many hematologic and solid tumors but minimally expressed on normal tissue. While CD70 was previously explored in MM (McEarchern et al, Clin Cancer Res (2008)), it was not further investigated due to heterogeneous expression in newly diagnosed samples. Here we revisit this target to suggest cellular therapies against CD70 could be highly beneficial in high-risk MM patients, currently the greatest unmet need in the field.

These identified list of protein groups were then median normalized and statistical analysis (two-sample two-sided T-test) was performed in Perseus.

candidates.title: Glycopeptide analysis of A549 cells after influenza A infection
candidates.description: Influenza A virus (IAV) hijacks host cellular machinery, but many virus–IAV interactions and contacting protein sites remain uncharacterised, particularly those dependent on intact cellular architecture, such as membrane-associated or phase-separated compartments. Here, we applied in-cell cross-linking mass spectrometry (XL-MS), integrated with AlphaFold-based structural modelling and functional assays, to map protein-protein contact sites in IAV-infected human cells.
candidates.sample_processing_protocol: Lysis of cells with a strong lysis buffer, then digestion with trypsin. Glyco peptides were enriched using PBA beads. Both full proteome and glyco proteome were pre-fractionated after TMT labeling and analysed with LC-MSMS.
candidates.data_processing_protocol: Generated raw files were searched using MSFragger v4.0 in Fragpipe v20.0 against the Swissprot Homo sapiens database (UP000005640, 20,443 entries) combined with the influenza A database (UP000009255, 13 entries).  For the quantitative analysis of proteomics and glycoproteomics data, we first normalized the TMT reporter intensities for glycopeptides and proteins with complete quantification across all conditions (i.e. TMT reporter ion intensity different from 0 for all channels) using the normalizeVSN function of the limma R package. We corrected glycopeptide intensities per protein by removing abundance-derived intensity using a linear regression for all glycopeptides with a matched total protein intensity. The corrected and normalized glycopeptide intensities as well as the normalized protein intensities were used for the differential analysis using the limma R package. For the design of the DE analysis, we considered the knockdown condition as well as the sample replicate. Contrasts were set for the comparison of the non-targeting control against respective knockdown conditions.

candidates.title: BioID2 interactome of wild-type SYCP1 versus the D918–942 mutant
candidates.description: This dataset comprises a tandem mass tag (TMT)–based quantitative proteomic analysis of proteins proximal to SYCP1 identified using BioID proximity labelling. Two independent BioID experiments were performed using distinct SYCP1 constructs: an N-terminal Myc-tagged SYCP1 and a C-terminal HA-tagged SYCP1. For each construct, full-length wild-type SYCP1, a SYCP1 deletion mutant lacking amino acids 918–942, and a SYCP1 knockout negative control were analysed in MCF7 cells. Biotinylated proteins were enriched by streptavidin-based affinity purification, and the resulting protein lysates were submitted to the EMBL Proteomics Core Facility for downstream processing and LC–MS/MS analysis, enabling quantitative comparison of SYCP1-associated proteins across constructs and conditions.
candidates.sample_processing_protocol: Cells expressing either N-terminal Myc-tagged or C-terminal HA-tagged SYCP1 constructs were cultured under standard conditions and subjected to BioID proximity labelling. Biotinylated proteins were enriched using streptavidin-based affinity purification, and enriched protein lysates were collected for mass spectrometry analysis. Protein samples were subjected to the SP3 protocol (PMID 25358341) conducted on the KingFisher Apex™ platform (Thermo Fisher). For digestion, trypsin was used in a 1:20 ratio (protease:protein) in 50 mM N-2-hydroxyethylpiperazine-N-2-ethanesulfonic acid (HEPES) supplemented with 5 mM Tris(2-carboxyethyl)phosphine hydrochloride (TCEP) and 20 mM 2-chloroacetamide (CAA). Digestion was carried out for 5 hours at 37°C.  Peptides were labeled using TMTpro™ 16plex reagent as previously described (PMID: 31738517). Briefly, 0.5 mg of TMT reagent was dissolved in 45 µL of 100% acetonitrile. Subsequently, 4 µL of this solution was added to each peptide sample, followed by incubation at room temperature for 1 hour. The labeling reaction was quenched by adding 4 µL of a 5% aqueous hydroxylamine solution and incubating for an additional 15 minutes at room temperature. La
candidates.data_processing_protocol: Raw files were converted to mzML format using MSConvert from ProteoWizard, using peak picking, 64-bit encoding and zlib compression, and filtering for the 1000 most intense peaks. Files were then searched using MSFragger (v4.0) in FragPipe (21.1) against the FASTA database of homo sapiens (UP000005640; ID9606; 20594 entries; October 2022) containing common contaminants and reversed sequences. The following modifications were included into the search parameters: Carbamidomethylation (C, 57.0215), TMTpro (K, 304.2072) as fixed modifications; Oxidation (M, 15.9949), Acetylation (protein N-terminus, 42.0106), TMTpro (peptide N-terminus, 304.2072) as variable modifications. For the full scan (MS1) a mass error tolerance of 20 PPM and for MS/MS (MS2) spectra of 20 PPM was set. For protein digestion, 'stricttrypsin' was used as protease with an allowance of maximum 2 missed cleavages requiring a minimum peptide length of 7 amino acids. The false discovery rate on peptide and protein level was set to 0.01.

candidates.sample_processing_protocol: AC16 human cardiomyocytes (Thermo Fisher Scientific, AC16 cell line) were cultured under standard conditions and infected with T. cruzi CL Brener trypomastigotes at an MOI of 10:1. After invasion and washing, infected cultures were incubated ± DDD85646 for 72 h. Intracellular amastigotes and released trypomastigotes were isolated by differential centrifugation and DEAE-cellulose chromatography, and parasite numbers and purity were verified microscopically. For metabolic labeling, cultures were supplemented for the final 16 h with 50 µM Click-iT myristic acid, azide (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Cells and parasites were lysed in Click-iT lysis buffer with protease inhibitors, clarified by centrifugation, and azide-labeled proteins were captured on alkyne-agarose resin using the Click-iT Protein Enrichment Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Resin-bound proteins were reduced with DTT, alkylated with iodoacetamide, and digested on-resin with sequencing-grade trypsin at 37 °C. Peptides from each condition were labeled with TMTsixplex™ reagents (Thermo Fisher Scientific), combined, and fractionated using the Pierce™ High-pH Reversed-Phase Peptide F
candidates.data_processing_protocol: Raw files were processed in Proteome Discoverer v2.5 (Thermo Fisher Scientific) using the Sequest HT search engine. Spectra were searched against a combined Homo sapiens (UniProt UP000005640) and Trypanosoma cruzi (taxon 5693) database supplemented with common contaminants. Carbamidomethylation of cysteine and TMTsixplex modifications on peptide N-termini and lysine residues were set as fixed modifications; oxidation of methionine and N-terminal acetylation were set as variable. Peptide-spectrum matches and protein identifications were filtered to 1% FDR using a target–decoy strategy and Percolator. TMT reporter-ion intensities (m/z 126–131) were extracted, corrected for isotopic impurities, and normalized across channels for relative quantification. Differential protein abundance was assessed using non-parametric statistical tests with Benjamini–Hochberg correction (q < 0.05). Processed datasets were imported into Scaffold DDA v6.5 (Proteome Software) for additional validation and visualization. Proteins were screened for N-terminal glycine motifs, and candidate N-myristoylated proteins were further evaluated using the ExPASy Myristoylator prediction tool.

candidates.description: This project describes the proteomic profiling of human epilepic brain tissue, alongside control samples. Raw mass spectrometry data, along with search engine output, are included in this partial submission.
candidates.sample_processing_protocol: Fresh-frozen brain tissue was homogenized in lysis buffer and beads. Protein extraction was done by adding lysis and digestion buffer with trypsin. candidates.data_processing_protocol: Raw MS files were processed with Proteome Discoverer 2.4 (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Spectra were matched against Homo Sapiens database obtained from UniProt. candidates.sample_processing_protocol: Tissue samples were sectioned using a microtome (7 μm thick), transferred into 1.5 mL tubes and deparaffinized by incubation with xylol for 30 min. After the addition of methanol, samples were vortexed thoroughly and centrifuged for 2 min (15,000 rpm). The supernatant was removed, and tissue samples were air-dried followed by resuspension in RIPA buffer with protease/phosphatase inhibitors. Samples were boiled and sonicated, followed by heating for 2 h at 80 °C (500 rpm). Protein digestion was performed using the Thermo Scientific™ EasyPep™ Mini MS Sample Preparation Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific, A40006) following the manufacturer's protocol. The resulting protein extracts were then subjected to reduction and alkylation steps. Subsequently, proteins were digested into peptides using the reconstituted Trypsin/Lys-C Protease Mix with an incubation at 37°C overnight. The digestion was terminated by the addition of the Digestion Stop Solution. Finally, the resulting peptides were purified and concentrated using the provided peptide clean-up columns. TMT reagents (0.8 mg) were dissolved in acetonitrile (40 μL), of which 20 μL was added to the peptides (50 μg). Peptide quantification wa
candidates.data_processing_protocol: Mass spectra were searched against all entries from the human UniProt Database (downloaded: August 2021) using MaxQuant (version 1.7.1.0). Trypsin/P was specified as a cleavage enzyme, allowing up to two missed cleavages and a mass tolerance of 20 ppm Orbitrap for precur sor ions and MS2 fragment ions. The product mass tolerance was set to 0.5 Da, and a maximum of two missed tryptic cleavages were allowed. Carbamidomethylation of cysteine was used as a fixed modification, with the oxidation of methionine and acetylation of lysine residue used as variable modifications. A reverse nonsense version of the original  database was generated and used to determine the FDR, which was set to 1% for peptide identifications. Reporter ion intensities were adjusted to correct for the isotopic impurities of the different TMT reagents according to manufacturer specifications. Missing value imputations were carried out from a normal distribution (width: 0.3, downshift: 1.8) using Perseus software. The normalization of reporter ion intensities was carried with an internal reference scaling (IRS) method.

candidates.title: Global proteomic determination of the poly-pharmacological effects of PARP inhibitors following treatment of high-grade serous ovarian cancer cells
candidates.description: Global proteome perturbations upon PARPi treatment were measured using quantitative mass spectrometry-based proteomics. High-grade serous ovarian cancer (HGSOC) cell lines (PEO1, Caov3, and COV362) were treated with IC50 dose concentrations of Olaparib, Niraparib, and Rucaparub to assess differences in proteome response to differing PARPi accross a HGSOC cell line panel.
candidates.sample_processing_protocol: Samples were processed in triplicate with urea lysis buffer (8 M urea, 75 mM NaCl, 50 mM Tris pH 8.0, 1 mM EDTA, 2 µg/mL aprotinin, 10 µg/mL leupeptin, 1 mM PMSF). 100 ug of protein were reduced with 50 mM DTT and alkylated with 100 mM iodoacetamide. The samples were diluted 1:4 with 50 mM Tris (pH 8.0) and subsequently digested with Lys-C at an enzyme/substrate ratio of 1:50 for 2 hours with shaking at room temperature, followed by trypsin digestion at an enzyme/substrate ratio of 1:50 overnight with shaking at room temperature. The digestion reactions were acidified and quenched with 10% formic acid to a final concentration of 0.1% followed by centrifugation at 1500 x g for 15 minutes at room temperature. candidates.sample_processing_protocol: KM12L4a colorectal cancer cell line (Fidler’s lab, MD Anderson Cancer Center) were cultured in Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM, Thermo Fisher Scientific, 31053028) with 10% FBS (Merck, F7524), 1% GlutaMAX (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 35050038), and 0.1% Gentamycin (Carl Roth, 2475.1). Cells were maintained in a humidified incubator at 37 °C and 5% CO2. Next, ten million of KM12L4a cells were seeded on a 75 mm equilibrated PAAm gel at approximately 1.5x106 cells/cm² and cultured for 24 h in a humidified incubator at 37 °C and 5% CO2. For starvation, cells were washed twice with 10 mL prewarmed DPBS (1x Thermo Fisher, 14190144) and transferred to a new Petri dish to remove runoff cells. The gel was washed again and incubated in 13 mL prewarmed serum-free medium for 48 h to eliminate serum interference.  Starved cell medium was collected, centrifuged (5 min, 140 g) to remove dead cells, and frozen at -80 °C. A 10 mL portion was concentrated 10x via freeze-drying and resuspended in 1 mL sterile MilliQ water for analysis. candidates.data_processing_protocol: LC-MS/MS analysis was performed using an Orbitrap Exploris 480 mass spectrometer coupled with a Vanquish Neo UHPLC System for peptide separation (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Peptides were analyzed with a 2-hour gradient using 0.1% FA in MQ and 0.1% FA in 80% ACN as buffers.  Mass spectra were searched against the Uniprot Homo sapiens database using MaxQuant (v2.4.2), with trypsin as the digestion enzyme and stringent FDR thresholds of 0.01 for peptide identification. Protein quantification was performed with reporter ion intensities bias-corrected for TMT reagents. Statistical analysis included Bayes-moderated t-tests and filtering for proteins identified in ≥60% of samples, with significant dysregulated proteins defined by expression ratio cutoffs of ≥1.5 or ≤0.67 and FDR ≤0.05. candidates.title: Proteomic analysis of Prote-a-Tac
candidates.description: The 26S proteasome recognizes substrates via ubiquitin receptors, a mechanism we leveraged to develop a small molecule ligand- and ubiquitination-independent targeted protein degradation strategy. Our proteasome-targeting chimera, Prote-a-Tac, links a proteasomal Ub receptor (PSMD4 or ADRM1) with a target-specific antibody fragment (such as a scFv or nanobody), allowing it to integrate into the proteasome and promote ubiquitin-independent   degradation. Cell pellets were lysed in 4 % SDS and 0.1 M Tris-HCl (pH 8.0), boiled, sonicated, centrifuged, and quantified by BCA. 40 µg of protein were acetone-precipitated, then resuspended in buffer with 5 % SDS, reduced (TCEP), and alkylated (CAA). After acidification, samples were loaded onto S-Trap columns, washed, and digested on-column with trypsin. Peptides were eluted, TMTpro-labeled, pooled, C18-cleaned, fractionated into 24 fractions, and stored at −80 °C.

This was followed by methanol/chloroform precipitation of 100μg of protein, reconstitution in 200mM EPPS pH 8.5, digestion overnight at room temperature with 1:100 LysC (Wako 129-02541), and digestion with 1:100 trypsin (Pierce 90305) at 37°C. Peptides were labelled by adding anhydrous acetonitrile (Honeywell AS017-0100) to ~30%, followed by labelling with TMTpro (Thermo A44520) reagent. A small amount of each sample (20ug) was combined to make a bridge channel. 1% of each labeled sample was combined and analyzed unfractionated to ensure labeling efficiency was >97% and that the samples are mixed at a 1:1 (total amount) ratio across all conditions. After mixing, labelled peptide samples were de-salted using a 200mg Sep-Pak cartridge (Waters WAT054925), followed by drying in a rotary evaporator. Peptides were reconstituted in 5% ACN 10mM ammonium bica
candidates.data_processing_protocol: Mass spectra were processed using a COMET-based software pipeline. Data were searched against the UniProt Human database (June 2021), using a 20-ppm precursor ion tolerance for total protein-level analysis and 0.9 Da product ion tolerance. TMTpro and carbamidomethylation of cysteine were set as static modifications, while methionine oxidation and asparagine/glutamine deamidaion as variable modifications. Peptide-spectrum matches (PSMs) were identified, quantified, and filtered to a 1% peptide false discovery rate (FDR) and then collapsed further to a final protein-level FDR of 1%. Proteins were quantified by summing reporter ion counts across all matching PSMs. Briefly, a 0.003 Da (3 millidalton) window around the theoretical m/z of each reporter ion was scanned and the maximum intensity nearest the theoretical m/z was used. Reporter ion intensities were adjusted to correct for the isotopic impurities of the different TMT reagents according to manufacturer specifications and adjusted to normalize ratios across labelling channels. Lastly, for each protein, signal-to-noise (S:N) measurements of the peptides were summed and then normalized to 100.

candidates.title: DMXL1 interaction proteomics from U2OS cells
candidates.description: To identify protein interactions with DMXL1, U2OS cells were engineered to either stably over-express DMXL1 tagged with mNeonGreen (mNG) or express HA-dTAG-tagged DMXL1 from the endogenous locus. Tagged DMXL1 was pulled-down by immunoprecipitation (IP) and IP samples were processed for TMT-MS analysis. As negative control, pull-down was also performed from parental U2OS cells. Each condition was performed in triplicate.
candidates.sample_processing_protocol: DMXL1-IP samples were reduced with 5mM TCEP, alkylated with 15mM iodoacetamide, and quenched with 10mM DTT. Proteins were digested with Lys-C/Trypsin and digested peptides were labelled with TMTpro reagent for 1h at room temperature and reaction was quenched with hydroxylamine for 15min. Equal amounts of peptide were combined and desalted using C18 StageTip. Samples were analyzed by LC-MS/MS on an Orbitrap Eclipse or Fusion Lumos Tribrid mass spectrometer coupled with an nLC-1200 or Vanquish Neo liquid chromatograph. Peptides were separated on a 100µm inner diameter microcapillary column packed with approximately 35cm of Accucore C18 resin (2.6µm, 150Å, Thermo), over a 90-min linear gradient of acetonitrile. MS1 spectrum was acquired on the Orbitrap (resolution 60,000, scan range 350-1,350 m/z, 100% AGC target, 118ms maximum injection time). MS2 was acquired on the Orbitrap (resolution 50,000, isolation window 0.6 m/z, 36% normalized HCD collision energy, 200% normalized AGC, 120ms maximum injection time). FAIMS Pro was set to -30, -50 and -70 compensation voltage (CV). FAIMS was set to -40, -60 and-80 CV for the second run.
candidates.data_processing_protocol: Spectra were converted to mzXML via MSconvert and searched using Comet against the human canonical proteome (Uniprot 2020-02). Searches were performed using a 50-ppm precursor ion tolerance for total protein level profiling. The product ion tolerance was set to 0.03 Da. These wide mass tolerance windows were chosen to maximize sensitivity in conjunction with Comet searches and linear discriminant analysis. TMTpro labels on lysine residues and peptide N-termini +304.207 Da), as well as carbamidomethylation of cysteine residues (+57.021 Da) were set as static modifications, while oxidation of methionine residues (+15.995 Da) was set as a variable modification. Linear discriminant analysis was performed and peptide-spectrum matches (PSMs) were filtered to 2% false discovery rate (FDR). TMT-reporter ions were quantified by picking the most intense peaks within 0.003 Da around the theoretical m/z and corrected for isotopic impurity. Data summarization, normalization and statistics were performed using MSstats.

candidates.data_processing_protocol: Proteome Discoverer 3.0 (Thermo Scientific) was used with SequestHT and Comet search engines for protein identification and quantification. Spectra were searched against Homo sapiens protein entries in UniProt, with a precursor mass tolerance of 20 ppm and a fragment mass tolerance of 0.02 Da. candidates.description: Wound healing, a multifaceted process, often leads to chronic wounds when disrupted. Predominantly, research in this area has relied on in vitro or animal models, which potentially oversimplify the intricacies of human wound healing. Utilizing labeled mass spectrometry, we quantified the proteome of full-thickness skin samples at both acute and late healing stages from legs of 14 healthy individuals. candidates.sample_processing_protocol: Proteins were extracted from biopsy samples using the ProteaseMAX/urea protocol™ (Promega) to ensure high yield. Samples were prepared by using an in-solution tryptic digestion protocol, including reduction and alkylation of S-S bonds. Later, they were subjected to a TMT labeling strategy, allowing for multiplexing of biological samples (up to 16 using TMTpro).
candidates.data_processing_protocol: TMT-labeled samples were analyzed in a data-dependent manner, using MS2 (tandem mass spectrometry) sequence-specific fragments of peptides simultaneously with TMT reporter ions used for relative quantification. For deep proteome profiling, high pH reversed-phase fractionation was performed on TMT-labeled samples, and 12 concatenated fractions were analyzed to reach 6-7000 protein proteome depth in a combined analysis of the fractions. Protein identification was performed using H. sapiens database. The detected proteins were filtered by applying a 1% False Discovery Rate (FDR) cut-off. Proteome Discoverer™ (ThermoFisher Scientific) was used to determine relative protein abundances in the sample groups, by setting up a TMTpro quantification method (MS2-based). The protein abundance ratios were calculated as fold changes using median values for each group. The p-values were determined using Student’s t-test adjusted for multiple hypotheses.

candidates.title: Quantitative proteomics analysis of UBR4 knockout A549 cell line
candidates.description: UBR4 was identified as a potential oncogene in lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD). In this study, we performed a quantitative proteomics analysis using tandem mass tag (TMT) 6-plex technology in UBR4 knockout A549 cell lines to discover an essential role of UBR4 in tumor growth and metastasis.
candidates.sample_processing_protocol: A549 cell pellets were lysed in lysis buffer (4% SDS, 2 mM TCEP, and 0.1 M tris-HCl, pH 7.5) by direct sonication (10%, 3 cycles, 5 s, 2 s). Lysates were heated for 30 min at 95 °C. To minimize interference from the reducing reagent, the concentration of proteins was measured using a reducing agent-compatible BCA assay (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA). Then, each sample containing 300 μg of total protein was precipitated with cold acetone. Samples were re-suspended in denaturation buffer (2% sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS), 10 mM tris(2-carboxyethyl)phosphine (TCEP), 50 mM chloroacetamide (CAA), and 0.1 M tris-HCl, pH 8.5) and heated for 15 min at 95 °C. The proteins were digested via multidigestion filter-aided sample preparation according to our previously described process.
candidates.data_processing_protocol: Raw MS/MS files were processed with Proteome Discoverer ver 2.5 (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA), using the SEQUEST HT algorithms against the Human Uniprot protein sequence database (December_2019). The database search parameters were as follows: full enzyme digest using trypsin (after KR/-) with up to two missed cleavages allowed; a precursor ion mass tolerance of 20 ppm; a fragment ion mass tolerance of 0.02 Da; dynamic modifications of 15.995 Da for methionine oxidation and 42.011 Da for protein N-term acetylation; and static modifications of 57.021 Da for carbamidomethylation on cysteine residues and 229.153 Da for TMT 6plex on any N-terminus. The co-isolation threshold was set to 50%. Six reporter ion intensities for TMT were corrected for isotopic impurities as provided by the manufacturer. Peptide spectral matches and peptides were confirmed by a Percolator based on a 1% false discovery rate (FDR). Confidence criteria were set to a 1% FDR at the protein level.

All searches were done against the human protein subset of Ensembl 92 in the Nextflow platform. MSGF+ settings included precursor mass tolerance of 10 ppm, fully-tryptic peptides, maximum peptide length of 50 amino acids and a maximum charge of 6. Fixed modifications were TMT-10plex on lysines and peptide N-termini, and carbamidomethylation on cysteine residues, a variable modification was used for oxidation on methionine residues. Quantification of TMT-10plex reporter ions was done using OpenMS project's IsobaricAnalyzer (v2.0) (Sturm et al., 2008). PSMs found at 1% FDR (false discovery rate) were used to infer gene identities.    Protein quantification by TMT10plex reporter ions was calculated using TMT PSM ratios to the entire sample set (all 10 TMT-channels) and normalized to the sample median.

candidates.sample_processing_protocol: Thirty-nine patients from the discovery cohort were randomly distributed into three batches (Table S2). Proteins were extracted from FFPE tissue specimens of these patients and digested by Pressure Cycling Technology (PCT) assisted proteomic sample preparation as described previously (PMID: 35931778, 33503446). Peptides from each of the 39 specimens, six randomly selected technical replicates (including three intra-batch and three inter-batch replicates), and three common pooled samples samples were labeled with TMTpro 16plex reagent (Thermo Fisher Scientific, San Jose, USA) (Table S2). The combined sample of each batch was fractionated as described previously (PMID: 33503446). A total of 60 fractions were collected by high-pH reversed-phase fractionation and concatenated into 30 fractions. After dried under vacuum, peptides were separated in a 60-min gradient by Thermo ScientificTM UltiMateTM 3000 RSLCnano System and analyzed using an Orbitrap Exploris 480 mass spectrometry with FAIMS Pro interface in data-dependent acquisition (DDA) mode. The detailed settings of MS have been described previously (PMID: 35110523).

Briefly, trypsin was chosen as the enzyme for peptide generation, allowing a maximum of 2 missed cleavages. The mass tolerance for precursor ions was set at 10 ppm, while the tolerance for fragment ions was set at 0.02 Da. Variable modifications included oxidation (M) and acetyl (protein N-terminus), while carbamidomethyl (C) was set as a static modification. Further analysis was conducted on proteins and peptides with false discovery rates below 1% that were quantified.

candidates.sample_processing_protocol: At least two adjacent 1.5 mm diameter cores were obtained from each MIBC specimen for proteomic analyses. Histologically similar, but distant, regions of a single tumour block were sampled in duplicate for the specimens included in the analysis of heterogeneity. The cassettes were then paraffin-embedded in a horizontal orientation to generate a block of cores. Each block of cores was scrolled, H&E stained and reviewed a second time for tumour content. Tumour regions across the length of each core were circled on the H&E slide, matched to the block of cores, and cored a second time with a 1.0 mm punch or 0.5 mm punch. The ‘cored cores’ with enriched tumour were placed in their respective microcentrifuge tubes for each sample.

candidates.title: Discovery and Development of CD70 As a Cellular Therapy Target in High Risk Multiple Myeloma
candidates.description: Even in the BCMA CAR-T era, multiple myeloma (MM) patients with high-risk genotypes have the poorest outcomes. We thus leveraged MMRF CoMMpass data to identify potential novel surface immunotherapeutic targets in high-risk MM. As described below, we focused on CD70, an immunotherapeutic target known to be upregulated on many hematologic and solid tumors but minimally expressed on normal tissue. While CD70 was previously explored in MM (McEarchern et al, Clin Cancer Res (2008)), it was not further investigated due to heterogeneous expression in newly diagnosed samples. Here we revisit this target to suggest cellular therapies against CD70 could be highly beneficial in high-risk MM patients, currently the greatest unmet need in the field.

rejected_material.title: Plasma Proteomic Profiling of Septic Shock and Acute Pancreatitis
rejected_material.description: Septic shock represents the most severe form of dysregulated host response to infection, whereas acute pancreatitis induces a systemic inflammatory response of initially sterile origin. Although the conditions share clinical features, their molecular profiles may reveal mechanistic differences between infection-driven and sterile inflammation. In this study, we performed plasma proteomic profiling using LC–MS/MS in patients with septic shock (n = 13), acute pancreatitis (n = 8), and healthy controls (n = 8). A total of 663 proteins were quantified, of which 231 were differentially expressed in septic shock versus controls, 83 in pancreatitis versus controls, and 29 in septic shock versus pancreatitis.
rejected_material.sample_processing_protocol: Samples were processed in a blinded manner to ensure objectivity in the analysis. Abundant plasma proteins were depleted by treating individual samples with Pierce™ Top 12 Abundant Protein Depletion Spin Columns (Thermo Fisher Scientifc; PN 85165). For each sample, the filtrate was spiked with sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS) to 2% final concentration, triethylammonium bicarbonate (TEAB) to 50 mM and DL-dithiothreitol (DTT) to 100 mM final concentration. Samples were incubated at 60 °C for 30 min, diluted to 1:4 by 8 M urea solution and transferred onto Nanosep 30 k Omega filters (Pall Corporation, Port Washington, NY, USA) to be processed via the modified filter-aided sample preparation (FASP) method (Wisniewski JR et. al. Nat Methods. 2009 May;6(5):359–62). In brief, samples were washed 4 times by 8 M urea, and free cysteine residues were modified by 10 mM methyl methanethiosulfonate (MMTS) solution in the digestion buffer (0.5% sodium deoxycholate (SDC), 50 mM TEAB) for 30 min at room temperature, and the filters were then repeatedly washed with 100 µl of digestion buffer. Pierce trypsin protease (MS Grade, Thermo Fisher Scientific) in digestion buffer was added at a ratio of 1:100
rejected_material.data_processing_protocol: Identification and relative quantification was performed using Proteome Discoverer version 2.4 (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The database search was performed using the Mascot search engine v. 2.5.1 (Matrix Science, London, UK) against the Swiss-Prot Homo sapiens database. Trypsin was used as a cleavage rule with no missed cleavages allowed; methylthiolation on cysteine residues, TMT 6plex at peptide N-termini and on lysine side chains were set as static modifications, and oxidation on methionine was set as a dynamic modification. For the total proteome analysis, precursor mass tolerance was set at 5 ppm and fragment ion tolerance at 0.02 Da (Q Exactive HF) and 0.6 Da (Fusion). Percolator was used for PSM validation with the strict FDR threshold of 1% in both cases. Quantification was performed in Proteome Discoverer 2.4. TMT reporter ions were identified with 3 mmu mass tolerance in the MS2 (Q Exactive HF) or MS3 (Fusion) HCD spectra, and the TMT reporter S/N values for each sample were normalized within Proteome Discoverer 2.4 on the total peptide amount. Only the unique identified peptides were taken into account for the protein quantification.

rejected_material.title: Neutrophil proteomic changes associated with sepsis
rejected_material.description: To identify potential targetable mechanisms controlling neutrophil degranulation in systemic infection, we investigated alterations in neutrophil developmental state under severe inflammation. We performed tandem mass tag (TMT) proteomics on neutrophils isolated from peripheral blood of sepsis patients. We collected blood from patients with septic shock at Bristol Royal Infirmary (United Kingdom, n = 4). For each patient group, we collected matched healthy controls (HC) from the same populations. We performed longitudinal sampling at days 1 (T1), 4 (T2), 10 (T3) and 25 (T4) post admission to intensive care.
rejected_material.sample_processing_protocol: Proteomic analysis TMT Labelling and High pH reversed-phase chromatography 100ug of each sample was digested with trypsin (2.5µg trypsin; 37°C, overnight), labelled with Tandem Mass Tag (TMT) ten plex reagents according to the manufacturer’s protocol (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Loughborough, LE11 5RG, UK) and the labelled samples pooled. A 100ug aliquot of the pooled sample was evaporated to dryness, resuspended in 5% formic acid and then desalted using a SepPak cartridge according to the manufacturer’s instructions (Waters, Milford, Massachusetts, USA). Eluate from the SepPak cartridge was again evaporated to dryness and resuspended in buffer A (20 mM ammonium hydroxide, pH 10) prior to fractionation by high pH reversed-phase chromatography using an Ultimate 3000 liquid chromatography system (Thermo Scientific). In brief, the sample was loaded onto an XBridge BEH C18 Column (130Å, 3.5 µm, 2.1 mm X 150 mm, Waters, UK) in buffer A and peptides eluted with an increasing gradient of buffer B (20 mM Ammonium Hydroxide in acetonitrile, pH 10) from 0-95% over 60 minutes. The resulting fractions were evaporated to dryness and resuspended in 1% formic acid prior to analysis by nano-LC MSMS
rejected_material.data_processing_protocol: Data Analysis The raw data files were processed and quantified using Proteome Discoverer software v2.1 (Thermo Scientific) and searched against the UniProt Human database (downloaded October 2019; 150786 sequences) using the SEQUEST algorithm. Peptide precursor mass tolerance was set at 10ppm, and MS/MS tolerance was set at 0.6Da. Search criteria included oxidation of methionine (+15.995Da), acetylation of the protein N-terminus (+42.011Da) and methionine loss plus acetylation of the protein N-terminus (-89.03Da) as variable modifications and carbamidomethylation of cysteine (+57.021Da) and the addition of the TMT mass tag (+229.163Da) to peptide N-termini and lysine as fixed modifications. Searches were performed with full tryptic digestion and a maximum of 2 missed cleavages were allowed. The reverse database search option was enabled and all data was filtered to satisfy false discovery rate (FDR) of 5%.

rejected_material.sample_processing_protocol: Cardiomyocytes differentiated from three independent human iPSC lines from healthy donors were collected at day 30 of differentiation through centrifugation and the resulting pellet was stored at −80 °C. Cell pellets were dissolved in lysis buffer, sonicated, centrifuged and protein concentration was measured by BCA assay (Thermo Scientific). From each sample 50 µg of protein was isolated and reduced with 15 mM dithiothreitol (30 mins at 55˚C) and alkylated with 30 mM iodoacetamide (15 mins at RT in the dark). Phosphoric acid was added to a final concentration of 1.2% and samples were diluted 7-fold with binding buffer containing 90% methanol in 100 mM TEAB, pH 7.55. The samples were loaded on a 96-well S-TrapTM plate (Protifi) in parts of 400 µl, placed on top of a deepwell plate for protein binding. After 3 washes a new deepwell receiver plate was placed below the 96-well S-TrapTM plate and 125 µl 50 mM TEAB containing 1 µg trypsin (1/50, w/w) was added for digestion overnight at 37°C. rejected_material.data_processing_protocol: LC-MS3 data from the iPSC-CMs generated in this study were analyzed using MaxQuant software (version 2.6.4.0). Searches were performed using default parameters, including a false discovery rate (FDR) of 1% at both the peptide and protein levels. Correction factors were used and extracted from TMT correction factor certificate from manufacturing lot #WF322713. Protein identification was carried out using FASTA reference files from the UniProt human proteome (UP000005640_9606 and UP000005640_9606_additional; release 2025_04). Enzyme specificity was set to cleavage C-terminal to arginine and lysine residues, including cleavage at Arg/Lys–Pro bonds, allowing up to two missed cleavages. rejected_material.sample_processing_protocol: HEK293T cells were grown to ~80% confluency in 10 cm dishes and subject to the following treatments. For heat shock treatment, cell culture media was replaced with fresh media prewarmed to 42°C and placed at 42°C for the indicated time. For arsenite stress, media was replaced with fresh media containing 0.5 mM sodium arsenite. For matched control-treated cells, media was replaced with fresh media warmed to 37°C and maintained at 37°C for the indicated time before harvest. For proteasome inhibition, 0.5 µM bortezomib was added to the media during the 1 hour treatment time prior to lysis. HEK293T cells from one 10-cm dish per sample were harvested, washed with ice-cold PBS, and collected by centrifugation. About 100 μg of protein per sample of cell lysate was digested, followed by Cys reduction, alkylation, and quenching. The samples were further digested with trypsin and differentially labeled with 11-plex TMT reagents (Thermo Fisher Scientific) according to the manufacturer’s protocol.

The proteins were digested with Lys-C and trypsin, followed by labeling with 11-plex TMT. The peptides were pooled and pre-fractionated by a basic pH reversed-phase liquid chromatography system into 24 fractions. To boost statistical power, it is necessary to increase sample sizes by combining patient-derived data from various institutions. However, this practice raises significant privacy concerns. We created this dataset comtaining 30 healthy donors and 30 patients suffering from focal segmental glomerulosclerosis - a rare kidney disease - and distributed them to three independent proteomics centers. This distributed data were used as a proof of concept to introduce FedProt - the first privacy-preserving tool for collaborative differential protein abundance analysis of distributed data.
rejected_material.sample_processing_protocol: Samples were prepared by three independent scientists applying harmonized protocol. Briefly, 10 µL of the blood samples were loaded onto depletion columns (High-Select Top14 Abundant Protein Depletion Resin, Thermo Fisher Scientific) to deplete the 14 most abundant serum proteins. Thirty micrograms of the filtrates were reduced, alkylated, and digested using LysC followed by trypsin, applying the filter-aided sample preparation (FASP) protocol by Wisniewski (Wiśniewski, 2018). The samples were subsequently desalted using Oasis HLB 96-well µElution Plates (Waters) and reconstituted in 30 µL of 0.1% formic acid containing 3% acetonitrile. The resulting peptide concentrations were determined using a NanoDrop Microvolume Spectrophotometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Subsequently, five micrograms of each sample, along with a pooled common reference sample, were labeled using the TMT-11plex kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific). TMT-labeled samples were combined into six sets, each containing five healthy, five FSGS, and one common reference sample and dried in vacuum. Ultimately, the six sample sets were fractionated (High pH reversed phase peptide fractionation kit, Thermo Fisher Scientific)
rejected_material.data_processing_protocol: Raw mass spectra were uniformly preprocessed and quantified using MaxQuant (v 2.4.2) software (Tyanova et al., 2016) for each center separately. The analysis utilized default settings unless specified otherwise. The experimentally acquired mass spectra were searched against a human reference proteome (Uniprot, version 2023_05, reviewed/Swiss-Prot entries only, 20,418 protein sequences). Trypsin/P was specified as the protease (specific mode), allowing for up to two missed cleavages. Carbamidomethylation of cysteine was set as a fixed modification, while oxidation of methionine and acetylation of protein N-terminus were allowed as variable modifications. Protein inference required a minimum of two peptides, including one unique peptide, with an FDR controlled to < 0.05 in target/decoy mode. The match between runs feature was enabled.
